results.title: Measurement Invariance and Multiple Group Analysis - The Analysis Factor
results.content: # Measurement Invariance and Multiple Group Analysis by Jeff Meyer 2 Comments Creating a quality scale for a latent construct (a variable that cannot be directly measured with one variable) takes many steps. One important step in creating scales is making sure the scale measures the latent construct equally well and the same way for different groups of individuals. When a scale measures a construct the same for different groups, this is called measurement invariance. There are two methods for testing for measurement invariance: multiple group analysis, and a simpler approach known as CFA with covariates. In this article we will focus on measurement invariance using multiple group analysis. Multiple group analysis allows us to compare loadings, intercepts and error terms in the groups’ measurement models. To have strong invariance, we need to show equal loadings of variables onto the latent variable and equal intercepts between groups. There is a multi-step process .The required steps are in this order: ## Step 1: Rerun the Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) model separately for both groups.If different indicator variables load onto the constructs across groups, we go no further. ## Step 2: After Step 1, we’ve established that for both groups, we use the same indicator variables to measure the construct. Run a single model in which the two groups each have their own measurement model. In the table below are the estimated loadings and intercepts for the male and female measurement models. You can see that all the loadings are the same between males and females, but the intercepts are different.But the chi-square model fit statistics are different. If the difference in chi-square between the two models is small, the factor loadings are considered equivalent across models. The metric model is more parsimonious because we are estimating one set of loadings for both groups’ construct. The configural model estimates different loadings for each group. ## Step 3: Fit the model with the factor loadings and intercepts equal across all groups. If the chi-square difference between the metric and scalar models is insignificant, we have group invariance. If we have group invariance, we know the construct is being measured the same across groups.

results.title: Measurement Invariance: Complete Guide to Cross-Group Test Validity | Cogn-IQ
results.content: Reviewed by: Xavier Jouve, Ph.D. Measurement invariance is the statistical property ensuring that a test measures the same construct across different groups, times, or conditions. Measurement invariance, also known as measurement equivalence, is a fundamental psychometric property that determines whether a test measures the same construct in the same way across different groups, occasions, or conditions. * Learn methods for testing invariance using confirmatory factor analysis. The most common approach to testing measurement invariance involves multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA). Invariance testing is fundamental to ensuring test fairness across demographic groups. Violations of measurement invariance indicate potential test bias, where individuals from different groups with equal ability levels receive different scores. Effect sizes for non-invariance, such as dMACS for mean differences or R-square changes, provide practical significance beyond statistical tests. Recent methodological advances include approximate measurement invariance using Bayesian methods, alignment optimization for many groups, and moderated nonlinear factor analysis for continuous moderators. Measurement invariance testing is essential for ethical test use but requires expertise in psychometric methods.

results.title: A casual but causal take on measurement invariance
results.content: Measurement invariance means that the same causal model can explain the data in all groups. It’s more that measurement invariance tests whether certain things are the same across groups, conditional on the assumptions that the latent variable model holds. Baader-Meinhof much Measurement invariance implies that all effects of the group variable on the items are fully mediated by the latent construct.More generally speaking (and still keeping things casual), measurement invariance implies that all group differences in the items “go through” the latent construct. To figure out the precise group differences in the items, we would still additionally need the measurement model (Latent construct → Observed measures); this would for example inform us that the latent construct has only weak effects on a particular item, which in turn tells us that the group difference on that item will be smaller. From a causal perspective, scalar invariance is violated if the group variable affects the item scores through some mechanism that is not the latent construct. In general, metric invariance actually seemed unproblematic in those data; the data were mostly compatible with a model in which the effects of the personality traits on the item responses are the same for people at different ages (equal loadings). But from my perspective, it’s true to the idea that if there is measurement invariance, that means that the latent variable does not tell the whole story that is to be told on the item level. But this actually does not violate measurement invariance (as tested in tests of measurement invariance), because all group differences are still mediated by the latent variable that is being modeled, reported mental distress: Teenage girls today may have different levels of true mental distress which leads to reported mental distress which leads to higher item responses (the “good” path that we would want to target); teenage girls today may have different levels of sensitivity to mental distress which leads to reported mental distress which leads to higher item responses (the “bad” path that some would consider spurious). From a causal perspective, measurement invariance means that all effects of the group variable on the observed measures are mediated by the latent factor.
